newsitem.title: USA: O.J. Simpson may return to witness stand Friday.
newsitem.headline: O.J. Simpson may return to witness stand Friday.

text.p: O.J. Simpson, who faced harsh interrogation from opposing attorneys in his civil trial last month, could return to the witness stand as early as Friday for gentler questioning by his own lawyers.

The former football star was on the list of defence witnesses for Friday but the jury was first expected to hear continued testimony from Robert Groden, an expert who alleges that a photograph of Simpson apparently wearing the same kind of Italian designer shoes as the killer is a fake.

Chemist Fredric Rieders, who specialises in identifying blood DNA, was expected to follow Groden to the stand, after which Simpson was due to testify as the last witness before the trial goes into recess for a two-week holiday break.
Because it was unclear how long it would take to question Groden and Rieders, there might not be enough time for Simpson to take the witness stand on Friday as planned.

There was no court session on Thursday but an alternate juror dismissed from the civil trial earlier said he believed Simpson was responsible for the deaths of his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman.

"I didn't hear the whole case but ... from what I have heard up to now, I would have to go with guilty," Gilbert Bustillos said on NBC's "Today Show." Bustillos, who served as an alternate on the 12-person jury, was dismissed by Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki on Tuesday for mentioning that he was on the Simpson case in a Christmas card to a friend.

Simpson was acquitted in October 1995 in criminal court of murder charges in the killings of his ex-wife and Goldman. He is now the defendant in a wrongful death civil suit brought by the families of the victims.
Bustillos said he found Simpson's recent testimony, in which he denied ever hitting his ex-wife, unconvincing.

"I didn't believe him, everything he said. He denied everything. He denied knowing about the cuts (on his hand), he denied ever striking or slapping his wife," Bustillos said. "Anything that they brought up negative, he denied or didn't know. That just didn't go with me."

Bustillos said he would have had an easier time believing Simpson if he had admitted losing his temper at least once. "I could have probably swallowed it a little better if he said 'I lost control one day and I backhanded her' or something."

Simpson, who never testified in his criminal trial, took a verbal battering from the victims' lawyers during three days of testimony in November. He sometimes gave statements that contradicted his own sworn deposition and he denied flatly ever striking his ex-wife, even when confronted with graphic photographs of a bruised and battered Nicole Brown Simpson.

His lawyers chose to delay their own cross-examination, and legal experts suggested they wanted Simpson to talk about the positive aspects of his relationship with his ex-wife and their children in order to leave jurors with a good impression to carry with them over the Christmas and New Year's holidays.

"They must convince the jury that the O.J. they know and love is still there," TV legal analyst Starr Jones told Los Angeles TV station KTLA. "They will want him to emphasise his relationship with Nicole had its ups and downs and that they both had (other) relationships ... that he was not obsessive and there was no fuse burning."

CNN's legal expert, Greta van Susteren, said she thought the plaintiffs would try to drag out the questioning of Groden and Rieders in order to pre-empt Simpson making a climactic appearance on the stand just before the holidays.
